For this release, the cost is $0.15 input MToK/$0.60 output MTok/$0.015 cache read MTok, In this case the predecessor is MiniMax M3 (not Flash), which was $0.30 input MToK/$1.20 output MTok/$0.06 cache read MTok. So a 50% cut to input costs and a 50% proportional cut to cache read costs (20% of input -> 10% of input) makes the ~70% cost reduction plausible. A 70% cost reduction is very funny in light of reports saying LLMs are becoming too expensive. That is likely due to the need to compete with DeepSeek V4.1 ($0.15 input MToK/$0.60 output MTok/$0.003 cache read MTok), which this new model still does not beat because DeepSeek's cache costs are still confusingly low, but it's pretty close.

stories.title_en: I built a drone with only one motor [video]
stories.title_ja: 1つのモーターだけでドローンを作った [ビデオ]

comments.author: TGower
comments.text: Underactuated robotics are so cool. In the hobby BattleBots community, there is a design where the whole robot only has a single motor, but it's able to move in any direction and damage the opponent, all just by controlling the single motor's speed. Most robots have at least three motors, two drive sides and a weapon motor. The trick to getting away with one is integrating an impactor into the chassis of your bot, using the single wheel to spin up to ~3k RPM, then by tracking the rotation angle of the bot as it spins, you speed up a little while the wheel is pointing where you want to go, and slow it down a little when it's pointing the other direction.

comments.author: leoedin
comments.text: A really neat concept. It uses a special hinge design, a magnetic encoder and torque modulation to control the lift of the rotor as it spins. Completely negates the need for a conventional helicopter's swash plate. The single motor does have the pretty major downside that it spins the moment it's in the air. I suspect a 2 motor drone with a tail motor would be a lot more practical. But I really like how mechanically simple the rotor hinge design is - it pushes all the complexity into the control algorithm.

stories.summary_ja: 主な議論点は、単一モーターで駆動するドローン（またはバトルボット）の実現可能性とその制御手法です。コメントでは、特殊なヒンジ設計、磁気エンコーダ、トルク変調によってローターの揚力を調整し、従来のヘリコプターのスワッシュプレートを不要にする仕組みが称賛されました。一方、機構が単純になる分、制御アルゴリズムの複雑さが増すことや、空中に浮いた瞬間に本体が回転してしまう欠点が指摘され、実用性についてはテールモーターを追加した2モーター構成がより現実的だという意見もありました。また、誤差を縮小すれば大型ドローンへの応用も可能だと楽観視する声があり、高速回転時でも速度変化でブレード角度を制御できる点に驚きつつ、テスト時の安全対策（例：リーシュ）をなぜ使わなかったかという疑問も呈されました。特に洞察に深いのは、ヒンジとトルク変調で機械的簡潔さと制御の高度化をトレードオフにしている点を指摘したコメントです。注目されたのは、制御の ingenuity と実用上の課題を同時に挙げた意見であり、コミュニティ全体としては革新性を評価しつつ、制御精度と安全性への懸念が論点となりました。
stories.editor_note: 単一モーターでドローンを実現したアイデアは、マルチローター設計に挑戦し、重量軽減とシンプル化を追求する趣味・研究分野での新たな可能性を示します。日本のロボコン系でも注目が集まりそうです。

comments.author: jparishy
comments.text: I've wondered if these types of casual open world, resource collection games-- which are basically a series of mini-games-- would make good model training envs. Each mini-game has a pretty simple mechanic that needs to be learned, as well as the navigation and interactions to begin it. Those could be pretty useful generic skills I think. One of my side projects is a game, and I've made it so agents can spawn off their own world shard to play in. There's a little Chrome-driven agent harness that can grab low res screenshots while it speaks directly to the game over the wire to control things. I've had Luna play it and it can drive around (you play as a bike) but it did struggle to play one of the mini-games (Disc Golf). My idea was that model trainers could run it an RL loop using the harness to get feedback data and screenshots to use, then reset the game world as needed during the process. A smart model capable of multi-modal inference on screenshots/game context at 30-60fps could be pretty interesting, and I'm sure it's coming. No idea how much it would generalize but would be fun to see done.

主な議論点は、RuneScapeのようなカジュアルなMMOがAIエージェントの訓練・ベンチマーク環境として適しているかという点だ。少量のゲーム知識を与えるだけでモデルの性能が大きく向上するが、トレーニングデータに含まれない情報については幻覚が多いという指摘もある。さらに、過去に自分でボットを作った経験や、色のランダム化でボットが破綻した話が共有され、ゲームの仕様変更がエージェントに与える影響が話題になった。  

賛否両論としては、エージェント訓練に適した「ミニゲームの集まり」としての可能性に期待する声がある一方で、汎用性が不明であることや、より過酷なPvP環境（例：UO:SA）ではエージェントがすぐに破壊されるという懸念も示された。  

注目コメントは、Chromeベースのエージェントハーネスを構築し、低解像度スクリーンショットと直接制御を組み合わせてRLループを回すアイデアを提示し、30‑60fpsのマルチモーダル推論が可能なモデルならば面白いと考えている点だ。これにより、エージェントが独自のワールドシャードでプレイし、フィードバックとリセットを自動化できる可能性が示された。
stories.editor_note: RuneScapeをベンチマークとしたエージェント向けMMOは、ゲーム内AIの行動評価を標準化し、強化学習アルゴリズムの比較基盤として期待されます。日本のゲームAI研究にも活用できるでしょう。

In 18 months or so my job satisfaction has gone from pretty high to abysmal.

comments.author: searls
comments.text: I suspect that many of the loudest voices pushing back against AI coding tools never practiced programming as a hobby or saw it as especially fun, and the fact their job is changing won't make them start now. I think just about everyone in the industry appreciated hand-typed programming as a job, because it was a pleasant enough craft to practice and for a solid couple of decades programmers were treated extremely well in comparison to the vast majority of other careers out there. Today, juggling a bunch of agents to do what you want them to do, figuring out how to verify their work, remediating problems, and spreading yourself thin cognitively—all the while looking over your shoulder at an increasingly precarious job market—is notably less pleasant for a lot of people. It sounds and feels a lot more like an engineering or product management role—something a lot of programmers would never in a million years have signed up to do voluntarily. I'm probably an 8 out of 10 on the cooked scale—I'm juggling a suite of ten iOS apps and haven't written or read a line of code in over a year—but I get where these people are coming from. I think the suggestion that they can reclaim what they've lost in this new job they've been loudly expressing distaste for by adopting a new unpaid hobby will ring hollow to them.

comments.author: austin-cheney
comments.text: Programming is still fun, at least if you are solving real problems and building real products. The part of programming that sucks the most is untangling ambiguity. In my current app I had an ultra simple proxy convention, but it sucks. I have since settled on a different single convention to cover 6 different scenarios of traffic redirection, but it was a challenge to distill simplicity from chaos of the wilds and write all the various tests. It’s moving forward faster now but it was like starting over to get this rolling. What I find is fun is building things that solve real problems I have. Then my problem is solved, I am paying nothing for it, and I can extend it however I want for any reason without downstream restrictions. There is so much AI still cannot do in software. If you ask AI to build a faster WebSocket solution, for example, you will get more of what’s already there. I have a WebSocket library I wrote myself 4 or 5 years ago. I thought it was fast, turns out it wasn’t. I wrote my own perf tool for it and had a defect in the perf tool that spit out wrong results, but that defect showed me where the performance bottleneck was. Now my library is 40x-100x faster than other WebSocket libraries. I did use Claude to analyze my earlier perf bug, and it made the same mistakes I was making. If you want to go faster than popular battle tested solutions you have to be original and AI just isn’t quite there.

But they are absolutely valid and enjoyable hobbies. And the skills they provide are transferable. Patience, attention to detail, staying on task.

comments.author: joefourier
comments.text: My field is primarily audio/vision ML so I don't have any particular domain expertise, but I don't get how you can lump all "time-series" together in one big bucket. My naive understanding is that the way to improve the accuracy is to gain as much joint information as possible. Like: > Known-future covariates. Some drivers of sensor behaviour are known in advance, such as production schedules, planned shutdowns, weather forecasts. Timestral can condition on them to improve forecast quality, so a scheduled load increase is expected rather than flagged as a surprise. To me this should be the entire basis of the system, not a condition to improve forecast quality? Like if you're modelling electricity consumption, if all you have is a window of N previous samples, you're going to get completely beaten by a comparatively simple system that knows the time of day, that there's holidays coming up, the weather forecast, etc. I would also think that these time-series forecasting models would gain from a sophisticated understanding at least the labels of the covariates? A 5M model has no idea what a "bank holiday" is, it just sees an arbitrary class go from 0 to 1, and won't have any useful inductive biases as to what it means or how to link them to other pieces of information. E.g., wouldn't you predict €/MWh of electricity far more accurately with access to price of natural gas (itself influenced by many geopolitical factors), breakdown in composition of production of each energy source, predictions about roll-out (requiring a sophisticated LLM capable of understanding news and their implications), etc. What's the use in trying to predict it from 2 variables and a narrow window looking back at just 8192 or 32768 samples? Or perhaps I misunderstand the use-case and this is more for extremely short term movements?

comments.author: logancbrown
comments.text: A lot of misconception around the utility of foundational time series models on HN. Sure, you could train a XGboost model on a time series with holiday or event covariates, but what if you have 10k different series to forecast for? You could train 10k different models, one for each series, but then they have very little history to learn from. Alternatively, you could train a single generic model to cover all 10k, but then you have to deal with scale mismatch between series in addition to the feature dev overhead between series. A TSFM saves a ton of work in modeling each of these series and could potentially generalize better to produce more accurate forecasts.

comments.author: kooi
comments.text: My question: What kind of dynamical system observability does Timestral provide? Is it a blackbox y = F(x, params) model for offline use? Can it provide the actual dynamical system equations? Or are you stuck forever querying the Timestral server (which is bad, think about if you're grid system operator doing day ahead, month ahead forecasts, and Timestral goes down) Typically, in linear, non-linear, and NN models, we fit some noisy data to A) An underlying model with unknown parameters or B) A model free search which attempts to construct combination of "basis" functions or C) A purely black box model which we only care about Input/Output error. A) is useful because often we know an underlying model we want to match, but don't know the parameter values. If we can determine the parameters, we get insights about the real system. E.g, how are these two variables coupled and how strongly -> We can make business decisions about what happens if we adjust some parameters. So what exactly does this timeseries foundation model do and provide? Maybe, the observability is that you have a forecast, and you adjust the covariates and see what happens. But one would want much more insights than a "executive summary" of the forecast. The important parts for me as a signals processing R&D engineer. > Classical models such as ARIMA and linear regression remain well-established tools for forecasting time series. These models are usually fitted to a single series and learn only from that series' history. > Deep learning models such as PatchTST add the capacity to learn nonlinear patterns across many related series, but they are still typically trained from scratch on each dataset, so what they learn doesn't carry over to new domains. > Time series foundation models bring the pre-training approach to time series. Trained on a large and diverse corpus, our model learns patterns that transfer across series, forecasting zero-shot on data it has never seen, even in domains where data is scarce. Edit: Looks like it's a pure black box which you can run on premise. > Output: Probabilistic forecasts, 21 quantiles > Inputs: Multivariate targets, past-only and known-future covariates

stories.summary_ja:
・主な議論点  
記事の中で「weirdly（奇妙に）」という表現が、AESにおけるガロア有限体と多項式の同値関係を説明する際に使われたことに対する疑問が中心となった。コメントでは、ガロアが本来目指していたのは高次方程式の解の解析的不可解さや正七角形作図の不可能性など、多項式に関する根本的な性質を証明することであったため、その文脈で「weirdly」と言うのは適切でないのではないかと指摘されている。

・賛否両論  
このコメント自身は肯定的・否定的な立場を明確に示していないが、読者の間では「weirdly」という語彙選択が誤解を招くか、あるいはガロアの思想を強調するための意図的な表現かで意見が分かれている様子がうかがえる。支持側はガロアの抽象的・直感に反する側面を強調するための修辞だと捉え、反対側は歴史的事実と乖離し、読者を誤導する可能性があると懸念している。

・注目コメント  
「I don't know that 'Weirdly' is right for the polynomial equivalence -- isn't that what Galois was trying to do in the first place (prove things about polynomials such as the impossibility of analytic solutions to higher order polynomials, and the impossibility of constructing a heptagon)?」  
このコメントは、ガロアの本来の目的と記事の表現の間の齟齬を指摘し、用語選択の妥当性について議論を喚起した点で特に洞察に富んでいる。

comments.author: nbadg
comments.text: For anyone else who didn't have "remote perspectives" in their personal technical lexicon: this refers to performing the ACME challenge/response check when validating the domain of a certificate signing request from multiple physical locations, and therefore via multiple physical network routes, in order to make network-level attacks more difficult. For example, if you were validating example.com, you'd need to set up some response to the ACME challenge somewhere, either through direct DNS-based validation (DNS-01, DNS-PERSIST-01) or through a server running at the resolved A/AAAA IP address for example.com (HTTP-01, TLS-ALPN-01). In all cases, when a CA goes to validate your challenge response, it relies both upon DNS and upon the network integrity between the CA's datacenters and your DNS and/or app servers. Both of these can be subverted, eg via BGP attack, to allow an attacker to replace a DNS response, re-route the destination IP address to a different server, etc, at which point they can inject their own challenge response, and therefore issue their own (unauthorized) certificates. Multi-perspective validation means that the CA validates your challenge response from multiple datacenters on different networks instead of just one, such that a hypothetical network attack would have to target multiple independent networks in order to successfully issue their unauthorized certificate. More info: https://letsencrypt.org/2020/02/19/multi-perspective-validat... https://community.letsencrypt.org/t/multi-perspective-valida...

comments.author: throw0101a
comments.text: In August an attacker was able to get a certificate issued even with multi-perspective validation: > For 33 hours in late August, a rival network hijacked a block of Hetzner-hosted infrastructure serving Softaculous and Virtualizor, using it to issue a valid TLS certificate and push a malicious software update. The stolen route was RPKI-invalid the entire time, on file, checkable by anyone. It still won on most of the internet. > At 20:57 UTC on 28 August, a network nobody at Hetzner or Softaculous had dealt with before started announcing 162.55.80.0/24 to the internet. It was a small, unremarkable-looking slice of Hetzner’s own address space — the block hosting Softaculous’s client area, its billing pages, and the update endpoint that every Virtualizor-licensed control panel on the internet periodically calls home to. For the next 33 hours, with an 11-hour lull in the middle, a meaningful share of global traffic bound for that block went to the hijacker instead. Some of it was Let’s Encrypt’s own domain-control validation, which is how the attacker walked away with a certificate for virtualizor.com that no browser would ever flag. * https://cloudpunk.blog/post/bgp-hijack-rpki-gap/ So it's all very well to have multiple network locations to prevent hijacking on the path (i.e., you have to attack multiple paths), but if the network as a whole thinks the destination is someplace else then all those paths will lead to the same (false) location. Perhaps the CAB should consider RPKI validation as a "MUST" rather than piling on multiple sources of validation who still have the same single point of failure (the spoofing of the destination).

comments.author: epsylon
comments.text: There's a lot of claim and so little technical details on that page. How was the formalization of Python accomplished? What formal proof framework do you use? How do you reproduce the optimizations across several instances / runs of the program? (since the source code doesn't change... assuming you don't redo the same work over and over?) What visibility, tracking and logging is there into the actual code running? Debugging is an extremely important part of building software, especially if there's a demon switching out binary code constantly underneath. Even if the recompiler is perfect (it won't be), user code never is. Why is the superoptimization and visibility into the data not surfaced back to the level of the source code? This seems like a waste.

comments.author: gavinray
comments.text: This was a lot more exciting than I expected. The homepage does not do a very good job of explaining what we're looking at: It appears to be a combination of two things: 1) A formalization of the Python language 2) An LLM which hooks into running programs and hot-swaps code with verifiably-equivalent behavior but better runtime performance, found via superoptimization and then verified via the formalization rules This is brilliant, and in hindsight one of those "I can't believe nobody had thought of this yet" sort of things.

comments.author: mccoyb
comments.text: Let me say that I like the idea: - verification - superoptimization specialized to a particular piece of hardware - patching binaries while they are running all great That being said, I'm getting some weird vibes from the prose on this site. Little phrases and claims that seem intended for the purposes of marketing, but conflate things with clear technical meaning in confusing ways. For instance: I watched the video ("a code execution model has to be right every time") which implicitly communicates something like "the model cannot hallucinate" ... of course, the agentic LM is still probabilistic, but it is wrapped with verification tools (to reason about semantic equivalence), and is likely post-trained to be good at using those tools. This strikes me as a conflation between the model and the harness which is intended to strike a marketing point (like: "it doesn't hallucinate") but which is clearly a ridiculous claim to make (falling down the slope: any harness which does error correction for improper tool calls might also be a "model which makes no mistakes") Also: "self-improving code" that's not really it, is it? Self-improving code would be code that runs itself and improves itself. This is code I run, which Maxwell watches and improves ... no? Related: I dislike the usage of the word "model" in the above discussions on the site. Do we want to call everything a "model" now? Can anyone invent a new frontier "model" by post training an agentic LM with tools? Also, let's say you are optimizing kernels on GPUs. This can be subtly fraught: for instance, it was well-known for awhile that one should only use certain pieces of software (vLLM, for instance) to reproduce papers (which used vLLM) there are non-deterministic sources of randomness (including, of course, floating point) that would prevent one from recovering the performance claimed in a paper ...

stories.summary_ja:
**主な議論点**  
- Maxwell が Python の形式化と LLM ベースのスーパーオプティマイザを組み合わせ、実行中のバイナリを同値かつ高速なコードにホットスワップする仕組みだと理解されている点。  
- 形式証明の詳細（どの証明フレームワークを使うか、Python の形式化手法、最適化の再現性・ロギング・デバッグ手段）がほとんど示されておらず、技術的根拠が不透明だという指摘が多数。  
- 最適化による演算量削減と、最適化探索や検証に必要なモデル計算コストのトレードオフについての疑問。  
- マーケティング寄りの表現（「幻覚しない」「自己改善コード」）と実際の技術的意味の乖離が指摘され、用語の乱用や誇張が懸念されている。  

**賛否両論**  
- 賛成側：形式検証とスーパーオプティマイズを組み合わせるアイデアは独創的で、実行時最適化の新たな道筋になる可能性に期待。  
- 懐疑/批判側：詳細が欠如し、再現性・デバッグ性・計算コストの観点で実現可能性に疑問；マーケティング語が技術内容を曖昧にし、誤解を招きやすい。  

**注目コメント**  
- 「形式化された Python と LLM が連携して、検証済み同値かつ高速なコードに実行中のバイナリを置き換える」という解説をしたコメントは、プロジェクトの核心を端的に捉えており、多くの参加者が「なるほど」と納得した洞察として挙げられた。

comments.text: I got hit with a cryptominer on my mac mini the other day. I only noticed because I happened to sitting in the room with it and noticed the fans were working overtime. There was a process, "icloud-services", which was using 100% of the CPU. It's sort of an indictment of Apple that my first inclination was "they've got a bug that's got an infinite loop" instead of "this is malicious software". After a reboot, I traced it back to a folder in `Library/Application Support` which included a `config.json` that mentioned gulf[.]moneroocean[.]stream, so I knew I'd been popped. Cleanup was easy enough (the files themselves, plus the launch daemon), but it's annoying. I don't do dev work on that machine (it's really just for plex & stuff) so it must have been some sort of vulnerability in Plex (but not the one described in OP) or macOS itself. Interestingly, I was up to date on my Plex install, but my macOS version was behind what was apparently an important security update related to an RCE (Sequoia 15.8).

comments.text: Testing. Lots and lots of testing. I usually interactively test with the LLM. Now that I'm spending less time, coding, I get to spend more time, testing. comments.author: spacedcowboy
comments.text: I’m slowly coming around to the idea that if it works, I’m good with that. I never used to personally check all my colleagues work, either, I just trusted that they’d done a good job. That’s not to say I blindly trust an LLM - my project is an autovectorising compiler. I have it write a bazillion tests, and I have real, non-trivial programs that it compiled. I have it run a ‘gate’ before releases that takes literally hours on 5 different architectures. To say this code is tested is … masterful understatement. I think what helps is a long planning session, going into details, working out corner cases, designing test-cases, you know work and effort. Once that’s done it’s easier to let it work through the night and do a major production feature. I still review the code, but hand on heart I couldn’t say I’d reviewed everything , sometimes I miss something in a complicated check-in. I try to keep checkins small and contained, but sometimes that’s not easy to manage alongside the “don’t break stuff” rule as well. So it comes down to: I’ve been working on this for 6 months or so, and so far this has worked out for me. You know, kind of like getting used to a colleague’s idiosyncrasies over a period of time. I will say that in my experience the code quality is fairly high. Maybe that’s down to the effort put in ahead of time in the planning stages, I don’t know, but I don’t seem to suffer from the ‘slop’ that people complain of. YMMV.

comments.author: solatic
comments.text: It's not too dissimilar to life as a Principal level engineer pre-AI. You technically oversee the work of many engineers on their own systems, but you couldn't possibly review all the code yourself. You appreciate that human code review reduces, but does not eliminate, the number and severity of bugs shipped to production. You don't have the low-level details in your head, just the high-level ones. You design how all these engineers interact with each other, without stepping on any toes. Time will tell whether we were right to move from a system where we trusted humans to understand the low-level system, to one where we trust fancy calculators. But so far, it's working.

stories.summary_ja:
主な議論点: ウクライナがドローンで負傷兵を空輸 evacuated したことへの称賛と、これがドローン技術の高さと兵士への配慮を示すという点が最も議論された。さらに、同じ日にハルキフでロシア製ドローンが乳児と女性を殺害した事実と対比され、敵対的使用と人道的使用の二面性が話題になった。  
賛否両論: 賛成側はウクライナの迅速かつ低コストな医療支援を肯定し、敵のドローン攻撃と対比して人道的利用を強調する。否定・懐疑側はヘリコプターと比較して安全性や積載能力に疑問を呈し、米国が弾道ミサイル警告を停止したことに不安を表明する声も見られた。  
注目コメント: ドローンで補給品も投下できるというアイデアや、ドイツ企業アビルスが示した医療搬送ドローンの実用試験状況に関する情報提供が特に洞察に富んでいた。また、「読んで感動した」という感情的コメントや、次の戦時発明として「空中地雷」を挙げたユニークな提案も注目された。
stories.editor_note: ウクライナでの負傷兵のドローン救出は、災害時・戦場での迅速な医療搬送手段として注目され、日本の自治体や防災関連でもドローン医療支援の実証実験が進んでいます。

stories.summary_ja: 「主な議論点は、CERNでの研究においてこれまで使える機械学習手法がブースト決定木程度に限られていたことへの驚きと、今回のMistralとの戦略的パートナーシップが科学者もAI時代に取り残されないようにする期待だ。さらに、欧州の大学や研究機関が連携を強め、欧州製AIプロバイダーを活用すべきという声も多い。賛否はほぼなく、前向きな反応が中心だが、一部からは過去のツール制約への懐疑や、資金不足への不安も見られた。注目コメントとして、博士時代にブースト決定_treeしか使えなかったというエピソードや、科学者が「置き換えられる心配」から外されないよう願う意見が特に洞察的だった。」

stories.summary_ja: 主な議論点は、投稿されたオープンソースの早期読書リーダー（フォニックス支援付き）に対して、コメント者が「面白い」と評価し、かつてジェリー・ポーネルが言及していた読み書き学習アプリが現在絶版かもしれないという疑問を呈したことです。さらに、そのような中間的教材として「Living Books」シリーズを参考にすることを提案しています。コメントは肯定的であり、賛否の対立は見られません。注目すべき点は、過去の有名な教育ソフトウェアへの言及と、現代のオープンソースプロジェクトとの関連性を探ろうとする洞察です。

comments.author: ttul
comments.text: I was chatting with a friend who commits on a very well known open source project (~80K stars). He is disillusioned not because the robots aren't good at what they do -- they totally are. The sad thing is that he enjoyed writing code and working with the community on improvements because it was a very human, collaborative thing to do. So, while the robots are great at pushing the project forward even faster and doing fantastic things for security and performance, the joy is gone. I can totally identify with that feeling. It must be how professional mathematicians are feeling as well.

comments.text: One thing that strikes me about what is going on: we have been promised this renaissance in software, yet, it been 2-3y of accelerated agentic/LLM development and I haven't see anything great coming out of the LLM developed software world that is worth looking at. Let's take open source as an example: No new 3d/2d CAD packages that are more capable than Blender/FreeCad/KiCad, nor Blender/FreeCad all of the sudden became much more capable than they were just few years ago. I also want to point out,that I haven't seen any new LLMed software in Electronic/ElectroDynamic simulation, something I would LLM to excel at, beyond what already existed before. No new software that is equal to Adobe Creative Suite (that Vibed coded replacement is trash IMO), No new Operating Systems that are taking over. No new utilities that are super useful in day work. We are using the same software, we've used before LLM arrived. Reverse Engineering became much easier, it is plus. Finding vulnerabilities also became much easier, another plus. Models are getting better. But where is the new cool software ? Edit: I will go even beyond OSS. M$ & Goog, who are DEEPLY Vested into AI, have access to the best possible frontier models and large groups of highly proficient engineers. Yet, Windows and Android are as laggy & buggy, as they were 4-5 years ago.

stories.summary_ja: 「OPがRubyのgemをアーカイブした理由は、LLMやエージェントがコード作業を加速しても、開発の喜びや人間的な協調が失われたと感じたからだ。コメントでは、LLMがセキュリティやパフォーマンス向上には貢献する一方で、新しいCAD、シミュレーション、OS、Adobeレベルのクリエイティブツールなど画期的なソフトウェアが登場していないと指摘され、AIだけではソフトウェア・ルネサンスは実現していないという懐疑的見解が多数を占めた。一方で、LLMによる脆弱性発見やリバースエンジニアリングの容易さは肯定的に評価され、「仕事が楽しくなくなったら去る勇気も重要」という意見も見られた。特に印象的だったのは「ベッドに誰かが糞をした後では寝られない」という比喩と、LLMを「Crazy Town」に例え、人間の創造性が不可欠だというコメントだった。」
stories.editor_note: Ruby gemメンテナンスからの離脱は、オープンソースプロジェクトの持続可能性とコミュニティの負担を示し、日本のRubyエコシステムでもメンテナ不足問題への対策が求められています。
